title: Trump 90-Day China Tariff Pause, Markets Surge
description_short: Trump 90-Day China Tariff Pause, Markets Surge
description_medium: After weeks of market turmoil caused by sweeping tariffs, Trump announced a 90-day pause on most Chinese tariffs in May 2025, sending stock markets sharply higher. The partial reversal was framed as a negotiating breakthrough, though critics noted Trump had created the crisis in the first place. The pause reduced the effective tariff rate on Chinese goods from 145% to 30%. Markets recovered briefly before renewed uncertainty about the trade war's end state resumed volatility.
description_long: In May 2025, the United States and China announced a 90-day pause on most tariffs after weeks of trade tensions. The pause cut the effective tariff rate on Chinese goods entering the United States from 145 percent to 30 percent, and stock markets rallied as investors welcomed the reduction. The temporary agreement gave both governments time to continue negotiations but left the future of the trade dispute unresolved.

title: Trump Tower Moscow Negotiations Secretly Continued During 2016 Campaign
description_short: Trump Tower Moscow Negotiations Secretly Continued During 2016 Campaign
description_medium: Michael Cohen told Congress in November 2018 that negotiations for a Trump Tower project in Moscow had continued into the 2016 campaign, later pleading guilty to lying about the timeline. The proposed deal required Kremlin approval, and Cohen said he discussed a $50 million penthouse for Vladimir Putin. Trump had publicly said he had “nothing to do with Russia.”
description_long: In November 2018, Michael Cohen admitted that negotiations for a Trump Tower project in Moscow continued well into the 2016 presidential campaign, despite earlier public claims by Donald Trump that he had “nothing to do with Russia.” Cohen, Trump’s former lawyer and fixer, told Congress that the talks had ended earlier than they actually had; he pleaded guilty to lying about the project’s timeline. The proposed development required approval from the Kremlin, and Cohen said he had discussed offering Russian President Vladimir Putin a $50 million penthouse in the building. The project never proceeded, but the concealed negotiations showed that Trump’s company was seeking a potentially lucrative deal with the Russian government while he campaigned for president. Cohen’s false testimony concealed the duration of those talks from Congress and the public. The disclosure prompted renewed scrutiny of the Trump Organization’s business interests in Russia during the election campaign.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Tower Moscow Negotiations Secretly Continued During 2016 Campaign
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Tower Moscow Negotiations Secretly Continued During 2016 Campaign

title: Iran Retaliates Against Bases
description_medium: On January 8, 2020, Iran retaliated for the U.S. killing of Qasem Soleimani by firing missiles at al-Asad air base in Iraq. Reuters later reported that 109 U.S. service members were diagnosed with traumatic brain injuries. After the attack, Donald Trump said he had heard troops had “headaches and a couple of other things,” prompting criticism that he was minimizing their injuries.
description_long: Iran launched ballistic missiles at al-Asad air base in Iraq on January 8, 2020, in retaliation for the U.S. killing of Iranian General Qasem Soleimani. The initial U.S. public response reported no casualties, but service members later described concussion symptoms and other effects. Reuters reported that Defense Secretary Mark Esper was informed on January 16 that troops had suffered brain injuries; the Pentagon said 11 were flown to Kuwait and Germany for higher-level care. On January 22, Donald Trump said he had heard the troops “had headaches and a couple of other things.” The remarks drew criticism from lawmakers in both parties and a veterans’ group, who said the description minimized the harm. By February 2020, 109 service members had been diagnosed with traumatic brain injuries, a number that rose as additional troops reported symptoms and underwent screening. The episode showed how the consequences of the strike became clearer after the attack and how the president publicly described those injuries.

title: Trump Says He Is 'Not Joking' About a Third Term
description_short: Trump Says He Is 'Not Joking' About a Third Term
description_medium: In a March 30, 2025 NBC interview, Donald Trump said he was “not joking” about serving a third term and that “there are methods” to do it, while adding that it was too early to think about. He called a scenario involving JD Vance winning and later handing over the presidency one possible method, then said aboard Air Force One that he was not currently pursuing a third term.
description_long: On March 30, 2025, Donald Trump told NBC News that he was “not joking” about the possibility of serving a third presidential term and said “there are methods” by which it could happen. He also said it was too early to think about another term. When asked about a scenario in which Vice President JD Vance ran for president and later handed the office to him, Trump said that was one possible method. Later that day, speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One, Trump said he was not currently looking at a third term. The 22nd Amendment limits a president to two elections, placing Trump’s remarks in direct tension with the constitutional term limit. His answer turned a hypothetical succession route into a public discussion of how he believed a third term might be pursued, while his follow-up statement stopped short of saying he was then planning to do so.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Says He Is 'Not Joking' About a Third Term
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Says He Is 'Not Joking' About a Third Term

notes: The linked Axios page returned HTTP 403. The supplied correction research gives the March 30 NBC interview quotes and Trump’s same-day Air Force One clarification; the corrected account omits the unsupported August rally claims.

title: Trump Defends Roger Ailes After Fox News Sexual Harassment Ouster
description_short: Trump Defends Roger Ailes After Fox News Sexual Harassment Ouster
description_medium: In July 2016, Donald Trump publicly rejected sexual-harassment allegations against Fox News CEO Roger Ailes, calling them “unfounded” in an interview. Gretchen Carlson had sued Ailes the previous week, alleging he declined to renew her contract after she complained of unwanted advances. Ailes and Fox denied the allegations, and 21st Century Fox opened an internal investigation.
description_long: In July 2016, Donald Trump defended Fox News chief Roger Ailes after former anchor Gretchen Carlson filed a sexual-harassment lawsuit. Trump told the Washington Examiner he considered the allegations “unfounded” based on what he had read. Carlson’s complaint alleged that Ailes declined to renew her contract after she reported unwanted sexual advances and also described sexist behavior by male colleagues. Ailes and Fox News denied the claims, and 21st Century Fox opened an internal investigation. Trump and Ailes had clashed over Fox’s coverage of his campaign, but Trump described Ailes as a friend and defended him while the allegations were being examined.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Defends Roger Ailes After Fox News Sexual Harassment Ouster
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Defends Roger Ailes After Fox News Sexual Harassment Ouster

notes: The linked Washington Examiner story documents Trump’s defense after Carlson’s lawsuit, Ailes and Fox’s denial, and 21st Century Fox’s internal investigation. It does not establish the later allegations, Ailes’s departure, or the settlements summarized in the input; those outcomes need additional sourcing.

title: Electoral College Certified Despite Protests and Faithless Electors
description_short: Electoral College Certified Despite Protests and Faithless Electors
description_medium: On December 19, 2016, electors cast 304 votes for Donald Trump and 227 for Hillary Clinton; seven electors voted for other presidential candidates. The National Archives records faithless votes in Hawaii, Texas, and Washington. Congress certified the results on January 6, 2017, after House objections failed to gain a Senate co-sponsor.
description_long: On December 19, 2016, electors met in state capitals and cast 304 votes for Donald Trump and 227 for Hillary Clinton. Seven electors voted for other presidential candidates, the most faithless votes in an Electoral College since 1872. The National Archives lists those votes in Hawaii, Texas, and Washington. Advocacy groups had urged electors to vote their conscience, but the final count left Trump above the 270-vote threshold. Congress certified the result on January 6, 2017. Several House members tried to object, but none could secure a Senate co-sponsor; Vice President Joe Biden, presiding over the count, ruled the objections out of order.

preserved_fields.title: Electoral College Certified Despite Protests and Faithless Electors
preserved_fields.description_short: Electoral College Certified Despite Protests and Faithless Electors

notes: The National Archives page confirms the 304–227 tally and faithless votes but does not document the January 6 congressional objections or Biden’s rulings. The missing source is the Congressional Record or a contemporaneous report on that certification session.

title: Floats Buying Greenland
description_short: Reports said Trump had discussed the idea of the United States buying Greenland, an idea dismissed by Danish officials and widely criticized as a colonial-style fantasy.
description_medium: In August 2019, reports said Donald Trump had discussed the United States buying Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Greenland’s government said the island was not for sale, and Danish officials dismissed the idea. The proposal was criticized as treating sovereign territory like a real-estate asset.
description_long: In August 2019, reports circulated that Donald Trump had discussed buying Greenland for the United States. Greenland is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, and its government rejected the idea, saying the island was not for sale. Danish officials also dismissed the proposal. The suggestion drew criticism for treating a territory and its residents as an asset that could be transferred between governments.

preserved_fields.title: Floats Buying Greenland
preserved_fields.description_short: Reports said Trump had discussed the idea of the United States buying Greenland, an idea dismissed by Danish officials and widely criticized as a colonial-style fantasy.

notes: The CNBC URL returned HTTP 404; the AP link is a general Trump news hub, not an article about Greenland. The remaining source text does not identify who first reported the idea or give a source-backed chronology of Danish and Greenlandic responses.

title: Trump Threatens to End Funding to States That Don't Comply With Immigration Enforcement
description_short: Trump Threatens to End Funding to States That Don't Comply With Immigration Enforcement
description_medium: Trump threatened federal funding for states and cities that limited cooperation with immigration enforcement. An April 2025 executive order directed agencies to identify grants and contracts for possible suspension or termination in designated sanctuary jurisdictions, while directing the Justice and Homeland Security departments to pursue enforcement measures as permitted by law.
description_long: The Trump administration threatened to withhold federal funding from states and cities that limited their cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. The January 2025 threats targeted sanctuary jurisdictions, including California, New York, and Illinois, and put funding for services and infrastructure at issue. In April, Trump signed an executive order directing agencies, in coordination with the Office of Management and Budget, to identify federal grants and contracts to designated sanctuary jurisdictions for suspension or termination where permitted by law. The order also directed the attorney general and homeland security secretary to pursue legal remedies against jurisdictions that remained in defiance of federal law after notice. State and local governments challenged the funding conditions, and courts blocked many of them as unconstitutional coercion. The dispute tested the limits of federal spending power and state control over local immigration policy, turning grant administration into a major point of conflict between the administration and sanctuary jurisdictions.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Threatens to End Funding to States That Don't Comply With Immigration Enforcement
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Threatens to End Funding to States That Don't Comply With Immigration Enforcement

title: Trump Refusing to Pay Contractors: Hundreds of Lawsuits Documented Including Tile Subcontractors and Piano Dealers
description_short: Trump Refusing to Pay Contractors: Hundreds of Lawsuits Documented Including Tile Subcontractors and Piano Dealers
description_medium: A 2016 USA TODAY investigation identified at least 60 lawsuits and hundreds of liens in which contractors and vendors alleged Donald Trump or his companies failed to pay for completed work or delivered goods. The claims came from small businesses and workers across his casinos, clubs, and real-estate projects, including a cabinet builder who said an $83,600 final bill went unpaid.
description_long: A 2016 USA TODAY Network investigation found at least 60 lawsuits and hundreds of liens, judgments, and other filings in which contractors and vendors alleged that Donald Trump or his companies had not paid them for work or goods. The claimants included carpenters, dishwashers, painters, carpet firms, plumbers, bartenders, real-estate brokers, and law firms. One example was Philadelphia cabinet maker Edward Friel Jr., whose company completed an $400,000 job building fixtures for Trump Plaza and said its final $83,600 bill was never paid. Other cases involved casino piano dealers and tile and carpet subcontractors who pursued liens after partial or no payment. The article also counted more than 3,500 lawsuits involving Trump over three decades, but distinguished the subset related to unpaid bills. These were allegations documented in lawsuits and public filings, not a finding that every bill was wrongly withheld. The investigation described how smaller vendors often faced the expense of pursuing payment through court.

title: Scott Pruitt EPA Administrator Corruption — $43K Soundproof Booth, First-Class Flights
description_short: Scott Pruitt EPA Administrator Corruption — $43K Soundproof Booth, First-Class Flights
description_medium: Scott Pruitt resigned as EPA administrator in July 2018 after a series of ethics controversies, including a $43,000 soundproof phone booth, taxpayer-funded first-class travel, and below-market rent from a lobbyist’s wife. His security detail also handled personal errands, while aides received raises through a process that bypassed White House approval. Trump continued to praise Pruitt’s work.
description_long: Scott Pruitt left the Environmental Protection Agency in July 2018 after months of scrutiny over his spending and use of his office. Among the reported expenses was a $43,000 soundproof telephone booth installed in his office. Pruitt also flew first class at taxpayer expense, citing security concerns, and rented a Capitol Hill condominium from the wife of an energy lobbyist at below-market rates. Reports said members of his 24-hour security detail were assigned personal errands. Pruitt arranged raises for two aides using a process that bypassed White House approval. At least 14 federal investigations were opened into his conduct. Donald Trump repeatedly defended Pruitt and praised his work as EPA administrator, which included efforts to roll back environmental regulations. The controversies connected taxpayer-funded travel and office improvements with housing and personnel decisions that raised questions about private benefit, official resources, and oversight of a cabinet agency.

preserved_fields.title: Scott Pruitt EPA Administrator Corruption — $43K Soundproof Booth, First-Class Flights
preserved_fields.description_short: Scott Pruitt EPA Administrator Corruption — $43K Soundproof Booth, First-Class Flights
